claims.text: Chemical short-range order typically suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys.
SRO produces nanometer-scale chemical-potential fluctuations that act as strong phonon-scattering centers.
Scattering caused by SRO overrides any phonon mean-free-path enhancement arising from local ordering.
CrCoNi is presented as an example of a concentrated refractory high-entropy alloy.
A homogenized CrCoNi-like solid solution can have a disordered or effectively random initial atomic distribution.
Thermal aging near 1200 K induces nanometer-scale local chemical order without causing long-range phase separation.
A temperature below the secondary-phase solvus can activate diffusion for SRO formation while avoiding precipitation.
Local chemical order in CrCoNi can involve enhanced Ni-Cr pairing.
SRO forms nanometer-scale domains of alternating atomic species.
These ordered domains create local lattice distortions and mass-fluctuation potentials distinct from those of the random alloy.
SRO creates spatially periodic variations in atomic mass and bond stiffness.
The mass and bond-stiffness variations preferentially scatter mid-to-high-frequency phonons, increase inverse phonon lifetime, and reduce lattice thermal conductivity.
High-entropy alloys exhibit phonon-spectrum broadening consistent with the proposed SRO-scattering mechanism.
The SRO-aged alloy will have lower lattice thermal conductivity than the disordered alloy.
The magnitude of conductivity suppression scales with the SRO correlation length and order parameter.
In the disordered baseline, phonon scattering is dominated by point-defect mass variance.
SRO or local chemical order has been observed or otherwise evidenced in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys.
The proposed suppression may fail when coherent precipitates enhance phonon transmission or when the SRO length scale exceeds the dominant phonon mean free path.
Higher thermal conductivity together with narrower phonon linewidths in the SRO sample would indicate an ordering-dominated rather than scattering-dominated regime.
